section_1.title: Prerequisites: The Sliding Window Concept (0:45)
section_1.content: Introduce the idea of a 'local neighborhood'. Before convolution, understand that data (like a 1D sequence or 2D image) is treated as a grid. We move a small 'window' across this grid to look at subsets of data sequentially.
section_1.example: Imagine a detective using a magnifying glass to scan a long scroll of paper one section at a time.

section_2.title: Defining Discrete Convolution (1:15)
section_2.content: Define convolution as a mathematical operation between two functions (the input signal and a kernel/filter). Explain the process: 'Flip, Slide, Multiply, and Sum'. Use a visual graphic showing the Kernel overlapping the Signal, multiplying corresponding values, and producing a single output point.
section_2.example: Visualizing a 3x3 matrix (Kernel) sliding over a 5x5 grid of pixels, where the central pixel's new value is the weighted sum of its neighbors.

section_3.title: The 'Effect' of the Kernel (1:30)
section_3.content: Show how different kernels act as 'feature extractors'. Explain that the numbers inside the kernel determine the transformation. If the kernel has balanced values, it smooths; if it has sharp gradients, it detects edges.
section_3.example: A cat's whiskers: An 'edge-detection' kernel highlights the sharp lines of the whiskers against a blurry background, demonstrating how convolution helps computers 'see' structure.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: Image Processing & AI (1:00)
section_4.content: Connect the concept to modern technology. Explain how Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) stack these operations to recognize complex objects, moving from simple lines to complex features like faces or animals.
section_4.example: A smartphone camera app: The app uses pre-defined convolution kernels to apply a 'Blur' or 'Sharpen' filter to your selfie in real-time.

section_5.title: Conclusion & Summary (0:30)
section_5.content: Recap the cycle: Input -> Sliding Kernel -> Weighted Sum -> Feature Map. Emphasize that convolution is the fundamental 'language' of modern computer vision.
section_5.example: Analogy: Convolution is to digital images what a prism is to white light—it breaks complex inputs down into identifiable components.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.0 + j * 1.2
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Convolution is a fundamental language.", "It maps inputs to useful features.", "Vision relies on these operations."]

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Convolution blends two functions together.",
            "We flip, slide, multiply, and sum.",
            "The kernel slides over the input.",
            "Each overlap creates one output value.",
            "This forms a new feature map."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Defining Discrete Convolution", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # 1. Define formula (f * g)[n] = Σ f[k]g[n-k]
        formula = MathTex(r"(f * g)[n] = \sum_{k} f[k] \cdot g[n-k]", color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_in_area(formula, "A1", "B6")
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # 2. Show function f and kernel g as arrays.
        f_arr = Matrix([[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]])
        g_arr = Matrix([[0, 1, 0]])
        f_label = Text("f", font_size=20).next_to(f_arr, UP)
        g_label = Text("g", font_size=20).next_to(g_arr, UP)
        content = VGroup(f_label, f_arr, g_label, g_arr).arrange(DOWN)
        self.place_in_area(content, "C1", "E3")
        self.play(Create(f_arr), Write(f_label), Create(g_arr), Write(g_label))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # 3. Flip kernel g horizontally, show in #FFFF00.
        g_flipped = Matrix([[0, 1, 0]])
        g_flipped.set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.play(Transform(g_arr, g_flipped))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # 4. Slide kernel g over f, calculate sum-product.
        # Just a placeholder visual representation of the slide
        brace = Brace(f_arr, DOWN)
        text_slide = Text("Slide", font_size=18).next_to(brace, DOWN)
        self.play(Create(brace), Write(text_slide))
        self.play(g_arr.animate.shift(RIGHT * 0.5), run_time=1)
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#7FFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # 5. Display result array in #7FFF00.
        res_arr = Matrix([[0, 1, 2, 1, 0]])
        res_arr.set_color("#7FFF00")
        res_label = Text("Result", font_size=20).next_to(res_arr, UP)
        res_group = VGroup(res_label, res_arr)
        self.place_in_area(res_group, "E4", "F6")
        self.play(Write(res_label), Create(res_arr))
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#7FFF00")
        self.wait(2)
